titre: A Course Taught Under Another Professor's Name
accroche: In 1916, a mathematician in Göttingen teaches under a colleague's name. Her theorem is now a pillar of physics.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1915, David Hilbert invites a young algebraist, Emmy Noether, to Göttingen to help him clear up a problem that troubles him: in the theory of general relativity that Einstein has just completed, the law of conservation of energy seems to slip away. Hilbert wants her to be granted habilitation (the title that confers the right to teach) but the academic senate refuses: she is a woman. Hilbert protests before the assembly: "I do not see how the candidate's sex is an argument against her admission as a Privatdozent. We are a university, after all, not a bathhouse." The assembly does not give way. From 1916 to 1919, Noether teaches anyway: the courses are announced under Hilbert's name, "with the assistance of Miss Dr. E. Noether."

## A Symmetry, a Conserved Quantity

It is under these conditions that she publishes, in 1918, the paper that settles Hilbert's question and much more: *Invariante Variationsprobleme* ("Invariant Variational Problems"). The result, now called Noether's theorem, states a general link: whenever a physical system has a continuous symmetry, a transformation that leaves it unchanged, there exists a quantity that is conserved over time.

The simplest example: if the laws of a system do not depend on when we observe them (invariance under translation in time), then its energy is conserved. If they do not depend on the place either, momentum is conserved. A rotational symmetry gives the conservation of angular momentum. The theorem is not limited to these three cases: it produces them all from a single principle, formulated in the language of Lie groups and the calculus of variations, two theories that Noether combines for the first time with this generality.

The paper answers Hilbert's question very precisely: the conservation of energy is not formulated, in general relativity, as in classical physics, because the symmetry at play (invariance under any change of coordinates) is not of the same type as the usual symmetries. Noether obtains this result by posing the problem in full generality, well beyond the case of relativity alone.

## A Paper Long Ignored, Then Made Fundamental

The paper goes almost unnoticed in physics for nearly forty years. The conservation of energy itself remains debated until the 1930s, before the discovery of the neutrino definitively confirms it. It is only from the 1950s on, when quantum field theory broadly adopts the language of symmetries and Lie groups, that Noether's theorem becomes a basic tool: now present in every textbook, from classical mechanics to particle physics.

For Noether herself, these two 1918 papers remain a parenthesis. From 1920 on, she builds what will become modern algebra (the theory of rings and ideals), to the point that a contemporary will write that the scope of her work is not measured by the results taken one by one, but by an entirely new way of thinking about algebra, which became the norm for the rest of the 20th century.

In 1933, as soon as the Nazi regime comes to power, she is dismissed, like all Jewish academics in Göttingen. She leaves to teach at Bryn Mawr, in the United States, and gives a weekly course at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton. She dies in 1935, at 53, after an operation. Albert Einstein devotes a letter to her in the New York Times: she was, he writes, the most significant creative mathematical genius that women's higher education has produced since it began.

carte.punch: Her courses carried a colleague's name. Her theorem is now in every textbook.
carte.idee: In 1915, Göttingen refuses to grant Emmy Noether habilitation because she is a woman; from 1916 to 1919, she teaches under David Hilbert's name. In 1918, she proves that every continuous symmetry of a system corresponds to a conserved quantity: a basic tool of physics.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: Complete biography, with the detail of the three periods of her research in algebra.

quiz.question: Why is Noether's 1918 theorem now considered fundamental in physics?
choix: Because it proves that the total energy of the universe has been constant since the Big Bang
Because it made it possible to correct an error in the equations of Einstein's general relativity
Because it was the first result in theoretical physics entirely verified by computer
Because it systematically links every continuous symmetry of a system to a conserved quantity
quiz.explication: The theorem is not about a particular physical constant or an error to correct: it establishes a general link between symmetry and conservation (invariance under translation in time ↔ conservation of energy, for example), which applies as well to classical mechanics as to quantum field theory; no computer is involved in its proof, published in 1918.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why does the academic senate of Göttingen refuse in 1915 to grant Emmy Noether habilitation?
choix: Because she has not yet published a paper on general relativity
Because she has just arrived in Göttingen at Hilbert's invitation
Because the subject proposed by Hilbert is judged too speculative
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text specifies that the academic senate refuses habilitation because Noether is a woman, which prompts Hilbert to protest before the assembly, comparing the university to a bathhouse.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Under what name are the courses taught by Noether at Göttingen announced, from 1916 to 1919?
choix: Under the name of David Hilbert
Under the name of Albert Einstein
Under a male pseudonym chosen by Noether herself
Under no name at all, as an anonymous course
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text indicates that the courses are announced under Hilbert's name, "with the assistance of Miss Dr. E. Noether," since habilitation was not granted to Noether herself.

quiz_supplementaire.question: From which decade does Noether's theorem become a basic tool in physics?
choix: From the 1930s, with the discovery of the neutrino
From the 1950s, with quantum field theory
Only after Noether's death, in the 1960s
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text specifies that the paper goes almost unnoticed in physics for nearly forty years, and that it is from the 1950s on, when quantum field theory adopts the language of symmetries, that the theorem becomes a basic tool.
